abstract: A multi-agent system can reduce latency on complex tasks by executing work concurrently. Several pioneering harness frameworks support multi-agent systems. However, the scalability of current multi-agent harnesses is often constrained by a central orchestrator’s capacity to allocate tasks and coordinate workers. To address this limitation, we introduce Agensh, a scalable self-organized multi-agent harness without a central orchestrator: concurrent workers execute a multi-agent cooperation loop, continuously gathering context, claiming and self-assigning sub-tasks, taking action and sharing findings, verifying results, and merging progress in an asynchronous manner. The loop is supported by the agentic organization infrastructure comprising three components: a shared workspace holds proposed, ongoing, and completed work; a message interface lets workers communicate; and shared context retains reusable findings and work intentions. To test the scalability of Agensh, we evaluate it on the five hardest ProgramBench tasks with GPT-5.6-sol (high). Scaling from 1 to 128 agents raises the mean final test-pass rate from 19.31% to 28.78%, an approximately 49% relative improvement. Larger organizations reach comparable test-pass rates earlier. On pandoc, scaling from 1 to 1,024 agents raises the final test-pass rate from 33.89% to 55.06%. Worker trajectories further show that different forms of self-organized cooperation gradually emerges and standardizes as the organization grows. These results reveal the number of agents as a new scaling dimension for multi-agent organizations to expand the frontier of general intelligence, offering a practical solution for complex tasks under hard latency constraints or time budgets.

sections.body: The paper argues that single-agent and orchestrator-based harnesses limit scale, because a central orchestrator's capacity bounds how many workers it can manage. Agensh is proposed as a harness without a central orchestrator. Workers run concurrently and asynchronously, sharing state through a shared workspace, a message interface, and shared context. The evaluation uses the five most difficult ProgramBench tasks with a 6h budget and no Internet access. Increasing the organization from 1 to 128 agents raises the mean final test-pass rate from 19.31% to 28.78%, an approximately 49% relative improvement. On pandoc, scaling from 1 to 1,024 agents raises the final test-pass rate from 33.89% to 55.06%.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Agensh replaces a central orchestrator with self-organized workers, and scaling 1 to 128 agents raises mean test-pass rate from 19.31% to 28.78%.

sections.body: Agensh layers a multi-agent cooperation loop over an existing single-agent harness. Each worker repeats five steps: gather context, claim a sub-task, take action, verify results, and merge progress. Claims are announced as `CLAIM` entries in shared context, and overlapping claims are resolved through direct messages. The infrastructure has three parts. A shared workspace, implemented with Gitea, holds integrated and in-progress work under version control. A message interface, implemented with Mattermost, carries shared-channel announcements and higher-priority direct messages. Shared context stores typed entries: `OBSERVED`, `FACT`, `FAIL`, `CLAIM`, and `PATCH_SUMMARY`. Every worker receives the same prompt except for its worker ID.
sections.heading: Multi-Agent Organization Harness
sections.headline: Each worker repeats a five-step loop over a shared workspace, message interface and shared context, with no central orchestrator.

sections.body: Results cover the five hardest ProgramBench tasks with GPT-5.6-sol (high), Copilot as the single-agent harness, and a 6h budget. The mean final test-pass rate is 19.31% with 1 agent, 20.68% with 8, 26.52% with 32, and 28.78% with 128, a gain of 9.47 percentage points. Figure 6 shows larger organizations reach comparable test-pass rates earlier. On pandoc, 128 agents exceed 30% at the 30-minute checkpoint, while 32 and 8 agents do so at 60 and 90 minutes; the single-agent run stays below 30% for the first two hours. On pandoc, the final rate rises from 33.89% with 1 agent to 50.94% with 128 and 55.06% with 1,024 agents, a 4.12 percentage point gain over 128 agents.
sections.heading: Scaling Multi-Agent Organization to 1,024 Agents
sections.headline: Mean test-pass rate rises with 8, 32 and 128 agents, and pandoc reaches 55.06% with 1,024 agents.

sections.body: Claude Code supports persistent sub-agents and agent teams organized around a fixed lead session. Codex routes delegated worker results back to the parent for consolidation. Kimi Agent Swarm trains an orchestrator to decompose tasks and schedule sub-agents. DeLM uses asynchronous workers, a task queue and shared context without a central controller. ChatCollab and SlackAgents place AI agents in Slack for coordination. Carlini's compiler-building experiment coordinates 16 Claude agents through a Git repository and task-lock files, with no orchestration agent. STORM replaces isolated worktrees with a shared workspace that detects stale or conflicting edits at write time.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: Prior harnesses keep task assignment under a fixed lead or trained orchestrator, while some tools coordinate workers through shared state.

sections.body: The conclusion restates the design: a shared workspace, message interface and shared context let self-organized workers claim sub-tasks, exchange findings and integrate contributions without a central orchestrator. With GPT-5.6-sol (high) and a 6h budget, scaling from 1 to 128 agents on the five hardest ProgramBench tasks raises the mean final test-pass rate from 19.31% to 28.78%, an approximately 49% relative improvement. On pandoc, 1,024 agents reach 55.06% from 33.89% with 1 agent. Larger organizations reach comparable test-pass rates earlier, and cooperation broadens from peer coordination to standardized workflows and role specialization. The paper states that this approach may expand the frontier of general intelligence.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: Agent count is proposed as a new scaling dimension, though every reported run uses one agent model.

sections.body: Appendix A gives the worker prompt used for the 1,024-agent configuration, which is identical for all workers except the worker ID. It covers Gitea and Mattermost access, the shared context board, and the work cycle for rebuilding a program from a reference binary. Appendix B describes the event-driven runtime: router listeners write events to a durable queue, a dispatcher delivers them to persistent sessions, and idle workers are prompted after 10 minutes. Appendix C lists GPT-5.6-sol with high reasoning effort, Copilot as the single-agent harness, and token limits of 272,000 input and 128,000 output. Agents launch one every 30 seconds in the first hour, then one every 3 seconds.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix gives the worker prompt, the event-driven runtime, the experiment configuration and the staggered agent launch schedule.
